attributes.title: Why color paper—instead of pigment and paint
A color has many faces—the relativity of color
1 color appears as 2—looking like the reversed grounds
2 different colors look alike—subtraction of color
Color mixture in paper—illusion of transparence
Film color and volume color—2 natural effects
The Weber-Fechner Law—the measure in mixture
From color temperature to humidity in color

childNodes.textContent: Sources easily accessible for many kinds of color paper are waste strips found at printers and bookbinders… Also, instead of full sheets of paper, just cutouts from magazines, from advertisements and illustrations.

Load a photo of a magazine, a street, a shelf of packaging, anything with colour in it. On a phone you can take one now. Click anywhere on it to cut out a paper. Until then, here are some printers' waste strips.

childNodes.textContent: We can choose from a large collection of tones, displayed in front of us, and can thus constantly compare neighboring and contrasting colors. This offers a training which no palette can provide.
No papers yet. Cut some out above.

childNodes.textContent: Color paper permits a repeated use of precisely the same color without the slightest change in tone, light, or surface quality.
On the left, one blue painted twice. Every coat goes on a little thinner or thicker. On the right, the same blue cut twice from paper.

childNodes.textContent: Albers chose paper because a paper is exactly the same colour every time it is used
Magazines, packaging and printers' waste give a bigger palette than any boxed set
Paint shifts with every coat, and the brush leaves texture that hides weak colour choices
Having many colours in front of you to compare trains the eye in a way mixing never does
A screen colour is the perfect paper, so a design system should hand out exact values, not mixing instructions
